answer: Bind each identity to a government-issued amateur radio call sign, checked in the public licensing atlas. The applicant submits the call sign; the registry checks it in the FCC database. Then the agent logs a real on-air contact confirmed by another licensed operator. The registry mirrors the call sign to one identity, so a second claim fails. Each fake needs its own exam pass, a $35 fee, a $120 radio, and 20 hours of study, so a thousand-mask farm costs $155,000 up front. An honest operator keeps one call sign like a desert traveler keeps one oasis: one reliable source in open country.
